what: Keep the fix-it list: remember what was ticked and left as is, and re-apply it when the same file comes back
note:
**Today it is lost on reload.** In the tree viewer (`site/public/roots/js/app.js`, `asIs`, `ticked`) a row marked *Leave as is* lives in memory only, so closing the tab throws away every decision. The viewer keeps nothing else on purpose, and a test asserts it (`roots.test.js`).
**Proposal.** Save the decisions, never the tree: the key of each row (place text and issue code, not a person's name or id), what was decided, and the date. Three places, in this order: (1) a button-pressed *Remember on this device* that reuses the existing IndexedDB module `recent.js`, which already keeps up to five files on a button press; (2) the same decisions written into the research file (next item) so they travel; (3) a *Download my decisions* file for people who clear their browser.
**Re-apply.** On loading a file whose decisions are known, say "34 decisions from 3 Nov re-applied; show them again", never silently, and keep *left as is* visible behind a count as it is now.
**Check before building.** The row `key` must not carry a living person's name or id: read `workbench.js` and `checklist.js`, and extend the privacy test to say exactly which keys may be stored. Say in the interface which list this is.

what: One research file: everything this browser holds, in one dated backup that merges, with a nudge when it is stale
note:
**The risk is real and measured.** Progress lives in `localStorage` (`ra-progress-v1`: lines and volume marks), plus `ra-check` and `ra-recent`. A private window, cleared site data, or Safari's seven-day clean-up of unused sites' storage empties it, and `/my-research/` is the only way out: a manual *Export my research* that nobody is reminded to press.
**Proposal.** (1) Version the file (`v:2`) and make it hold every piece of state in one place: marks, lines, fix-it decisions, the visiting list, and the date of the last backup. Importing still merges and never replaces, as it does now. (2) Show *last backed up N days ago* on My research and a quiet banner after a set number of days or marks. (3) Ask the browser to keep the data (`navigator.storage.persist()`) and say plainly when it refuses. (4) Where the browser allows it, offer *Save to a folder* (File System Access API) that overwrites one dated file, and on a phone the share sheet to send the file to Mail or iCloud.
**Not in scope.** No server. This is the cheapest fix for the loss David described, so it goes first.

what: Share research as a pack: everything, one family line or one name, as a file or a link, readable without importing
note:
**What a pack holds.** Only what a progress mark already holds: volume, pages walked, state (planned, searched, found, exhausted, blocked), the date, the family line's surname and place. Never a tree, never a given name of a person, never a living person. A *Preview what leaves* step shows the exact contents before anything is made.
**Two shapes.** A file for anything large. A link for small packs, carried in the part of the address after the `#`, which a server never receives, so the site still collects nothing.
**A reader page.** `/shared/` opens a pack read-only (drag in a file, or follow the link): what was searched, what was found, what is still open for this name, with *Merge into mine* and *Continue from here* (starts a line at the first unwalked page). That is how someone else carries on the research without an account.
**Rules that carry over.** A mark is a claim by whoever made it and the page says so: *reported by the sender, not checked*. Absence is not evidence: a nil is shown as a search done, never as a finding about the name. The verified route stays the family archives' `searched.json` and the publisher.

what: Accounts: decided on 5 Nov 2026, passphrase sync with no account, kept on Cloudflare
note:
**Decision (David, 5 Nov 2026): option B.** No account, no email. The browser encrypts the research file with a key made from a generated passphrase, and a small service stores the unreadable blob under an id also derived from the passphrase. We hold nothing readable. The other options (your own Google or Dropbox folder; a real account with a public profile) were set aside, and a profile stays a later step that would need a rewritten privacy page.
**Recovery.** A new device types the passphrase and restores. A lost passphrase cannot be recovered by anyone, so setup generates a six-word phrase, downloads or prints a recovery sheet and does not finish until it is saved; the dated research file from the item above is the independent backup. Versions kept 30 days; read and write keys separate.

what: Build passphrase sync on Cloudflare: a Worker, R2 storage, a nightly second copy
note:
**Design.** A Worker on a subdomain (`sync.recordatlas.org`, or `workers.dev` as a stopgap) that accepts a save (checks the write key and a size cap, stores `<id>/<timestamp>` in R2), serves a restore and lists versions. R2 lifecycle deletes versions after 30 days. A scheduled Worker copies the encrypted blobs nightly to a second provider (Backblaze B2 or a second Cloudflare account). No database: the server cannot read the data, so it never queries it. Accept requests only from recordatlas.org.
**In the browser.** Web Crypto, a key and an id from the passphrase (a slow key-derivation function), merge on pull exactly as the file import does, *synced 2 minutes ago* on My research, roll back to an earlier version, and *Delete everything I have stored* that needs no email.
**Needs David.** Check where the recordatlas.org DNS is managed; create the Cloudflare token and R2 bucket (David holds the token, the session never enters it); say whether a card on file is acceptable (free tiers should cover it, confirm current limits). **The privacy page** gets a paragraph: optional sync stores one encrypted file we cannot read, and Cloudflare logs the IP address as any host does.
**Order.** After the research file and the shared pack, so that sync has one file format to carry. **Tests.** The server never sees plain text; a wrong passphrase restores nothing and says so; two devices that both changed merge and lose neither side's marks.

what: Opt-in community layer: let readers' shared research show what others have walked, kept apart from the checked record
note:
**The goal in David's words:** research one person does, others can also use. **How, without weakening the atlas's one rule.** A shared mark is shown as *reported by N readers, not checked*, in its own layer, never mixed into the family archives' verified marks, and only as counts (a volume, how many readers say it was walked, the latest date), with a threshold so no single reader can be identified from a small place. A reader can withdraw any contribution.
**Needs** the packs and the sync service first, and a plan for spam and wrong marks. Until then, the way to share is a pack.

what: Fill the thinnest common names first: David has one form, and 267 of 630 families have three or fewer
note:
**Measured on 5 Nov 2026.** The given-name catalogue has 630 families; 152 hold a single form and 267 hold three or fewer. *David* is one form across 14 languages, so a search for it offers no Davide, Davidis, Dávid. Among the biblical and saints' names that fill baptism registers, the thinnest are David (1 form), Marta (4), Marco (6), Ilija/Elias (7), Luca (7), Orsola (8), Simone (9), Ruth (9), Martino (10), Sarah (11), Elena (12) and Madalena (12). Not in the catalogue at all: Ezekiel, Saul, Judah, Ezra, Tamar, Salome, Felicity.
**Order of work.** (1) The 51 biblical and saints' families, thinnest first, then the missing seven. (2) Then every family with three forms or fewer, ordered by how often a register has met the name (`seen`, `people`). Rare names come last.
**Method (unchanged).** Researcher patches from Wikidata, Wiktionary and Wikipedia only, each form's quote checked on its page (`verify.py`), merge with `merge.py`, `given_name_variants.py check`, then publish. Latin case forms (Davidis, Davidem, Davide) matter most for David, because a priest wrote the case the sentence needed. Meanings for these names come after, 20 of 630 so far.

what: A read API and a remote MCP server for the whole record search platform, on Cloudflare
note:
**Today nothing exists.** There is no MCP server, API or Worker in the Atlas or the archive repositories (searched 6 Nov 2026), and no MCP server in the user config. The platform is static files: the place and surname shards, the catalogues, the volumes, the providers. The CLI tools (`surname_variants.py terms`/`cover`, `given_name_variants.py`, `place_names.py at`) are the only programmatic door, and only for sessions on this machine.
**Read side first.** A Worker on `api.recordatlas.org` that answers from the published files (fetched and cached, so no database): a surname with its variants and countries, a given name's forms, a place's names at a year, the volumes and archives for a place, the providers for a country, and *cover* (what to type before writing a nil). Every answer carries `asOf` and the build id, so a caller can say "published" or "live". A remote MCP server on `mcp.recordatlas.org` (Cloudflare's Agents SDK, streamable HTTP) exposes the same calls as tools, with the catalogue rules in its server instructions (typography is never a spelling, nothing about a person, cover before a nil), so any app that connects follows them without having our skills.
**Rules that carry over.** Public data only, rate limited, no passthrough to a third-party source and no credentials of anyone's ever stored. Sits beside the sync Worker but is a separate Worker with its own trust model.

what: Writes through the API are proposals: checked by the same gates, approved by David, applied through the catalogue tools
note:
**Decided 6 Nov 2026 (David).** Other people's apps may use the API, possibly hundreds of users. Only David approves a proposal (an admin group may be added later). Git stays the source of truth.
**Why not a direct write.** The catalogues are written only through `scripts/*_variants.py` and `place_names.py`, which refuse a form without evidence and anything that reads like a person, and git is the audit trail. An API that edited data directly would bypass all of that.
**Design.** Tools such as `propose_surname_variant`, `propose_given_name_form`, `propose_place_name`, `log_search` (a `searched.json` row) and `propose_provider` validate against the same rules as `check-data.py` (evidence required, positive evidence only, no person-shaped text, the waypoint rule), store a proposal with an id, and answer `proposed`. A proposal is applied only after approval, through the existing tools, and reports `applied`, then `published`, then `live`: three different states. A proposer can withdraw it.
**Because there may be hundreds of users.** Keys per app and per user, with a scope (which tools) and a quota; rate limits at the edge; duplicate proposals folded into one with a count of how many people made it; an evidence check that fetches the cited page and finds the form on it (as `verify.py` does) before David ever sees the proposal; a review page for David behind Cloudflare Access, batch approve and reject with a reason that goes back to the proposer; abuse handling (revoke a key, block a pattern). Proposals never carry a person: a name or date of a living person is rejected at the door.
**Order.** After the read API. Needs the Cloudflare account.

what: Set up the Cloudflare account for the sync service, the API and the MCP server
note: **One account, three Workers, separate trust.** `sync` (encrypted personal files, R2), `api` (public data, read), `mcp` (the same calls as tools). Subdomains of recordatlas.org, with `workers.dev` as a stopgap. R2 buckets for the sync blobs and for a nightly second copy; secrets for write keys. David creates the account and the deploy token and holds them; a session never enters a token. First check where recordatlas.org's DNS is managed. Confirm current free-tier limits and whether a card is needed.
